title: Computer Vision Lab
brandLine: NKU AI Native Studio × Cincinnati Museum Center

welcome.eyebrow: NKU AI DAY · COMPUTER VISION LAB
welcome.headline: Can the AI tell what it’s looking at?
welcome.body: Test a trained object, challenge it with something similar, then remove the object completely. Your results will help us think about how computer vision should—or should not—be used in a museum experience.

privacy.body: Camera images stay on your device. Anonymous interaction results and feedback are recorded for this prototype study.

artifacts.name: Target Object
artifacts.physicalObjectName: The object used to train the model

notice.question: What happened when the model looked at the trained target object?

discover.title: Recognition is a testable claim.
discover.text: A model can appear confident and still be wrong. What matters is whether it behaves correctly across target objects, similar objects, and backgrounds—not just whether it recognizes one training example.
discover.uncertainty: Today’s model is a prototype. False positives and misses are useful evidence about what would need to improve before museum use.

next.label: Similar Object Challenge
next.direction: Pick up the similar-looking object and test whether the model rejects it.

artifacts.labInstruction: Place the trained Target Object inside the camera box.

artifacts.name: Similar Object Challenge
artifacts.physicalObjectName: A different object that looks somewhat similar
artifacts.scenarioLabel: Expected result: reject the similar object

notice.question: What did the model do with the similar-looking object?

discover.title: Similar objects expose false positives.
discover.text: If the model mistakes this object for the target, it may be relying on broad visual features such as shape, texture, or color rather than the exact object identity.
discover.uncertainty: That does not make the experiment useless—it tells us where this recognition approach breaks down.

next.label: Background Test
next.direction: Remove the objects from view and point the camera at the table or surrounding background.

artifacts.labInstruction: Replace it with the Similar Object and keep that object centered in the camera box.

artifacts.name: Background Test
artifacts.physicalObjectName: No target object in the camera view

notice.question: What happened when no target object was in view?

choices.label: It still called it the target

discover.title: A useful model needs to know when to say “not this.”
discover.text: For a museum experience, false positives matter because a visitor may point the camera at the wrong object, a display case, another visitor, or the floor.
discover.uncertainty: Reliable rejection may require a different recognition approach, more targeted training, or a simpler interaction design.

next.label: CMC Reflection
next.direction: Finish by telling us whether computer vision would improve this kind of museum experience.

artifacts.labInstruction: Remove all objects from view and point the camera at the table or surrounding background.

finale.title: Experiment complete
finale.headline: You just stress-tested a computer vision prototype.
finale.body: Your results help us evaluate not only whether recognition works, but whether it creates enough visitor value to justify its complexity in a museum setting.
finale.closeNote: Thanks for helping us test the idea.

about.headline: What are we learning for Cincinnati Museum Center?
about.intro: This Computer Vision Lab uses test objects from a personal collection—not Cincinnati Museum Center artifacts. The goal is to let students experience object recognition firsthand while generating evidence for the CMC project.
about.section1Body: Can a model reliably recognize the intended physical object while rejecting similar objects and backgrounds? Today’s test intentionally includes both easy and difficult cases.
about.section2Body: If recognition works, does it actually improve the experience? Does it help people engage with the physical object, or does the technology create confusion and friction?
about.section3Body: The field study helps the AI Native Studio compare computer vision with simpler alternatives such as QR codes or manual object selection before recommending what belongs in the final museum experience.
